REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: Well, I try to – in my case, I try to show – I try to do what's right, whether it's President Trump's position or not his position.

And I just try to look voters in the eye that say, hey, I support Ukraine. I think tariffs are a mistake. I have votes to back it up.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: I also support the fact that we secured the border.

I support generally what we're doing in Iran, because Iran has been…

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: … waging war against us for 47 years.

So, I just try to call balls and strikes, and I try to be honest, and I try to do, once I'm elected, what I campaign on.

MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, well, we'll let you call some of those balls and strikes on the other side of this commercial break that I have to take. So, please stay with us.

We have more questions for Congressman Bacon and a lot more Face the Nation. Stay with us.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will be right back with a lot more Face the Nation with Congressmen Bacon and more questions. Should the government regulate artificial intelligence?

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to "FACE THE NATION."

We return now to our conversation with Nebraska Republican Congressman Don Bacon.

Congressman, I want to go to Europe and talk about Ukraine but let me first ask you about what was said at Normandy on Saturday.

Secretary Hegseth seemed, in his remarks, to link immigration to the legacy of the D-Day landings by allied forces who were liberating Europe from the Nazis.

Take a listen.

(BEGIN VC)

PETE HEGSETH, DEFENSE SECRETARY: Sadly, today, different European beaches are stormed by different, dangerous ideologies. Beaches in Spain and Italy and Greece and Bulgaria, boats and men arrive. When will European capitals do something about that invasion?

(END VC)

MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm not sure who the allies were in that analogy, but I wonder what you make of Hegseth's remarks?

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON (R-NE): You know, Normandy's a time to celebrate a great day. You know, it was – I've been on the beaches of Omaha. And, you know, we lost about 3,000 troops on that beach on one day. That's where the focus should have been. It's a chance to celebrate with our allies. We worked together to defeat Nazi Germany.

And one of the concerns that many of us have when it comes to this administration and particularly the Pentagon right now, they're very critical of Europe. They're critical of the E.U. They're critical of NATO. They're critical of a lot of the countries that make up NATO. And you never hear them criticize Russia. And that bothers us. Why are they so weak on the Russia, which affects Ukraine foreign policy, their policy toward the Baltics.

What they are quick to always want to criticize Europe. It reminds me of the message that Secretary Hegseth sent to the vice president on Signal when he said how much he loathed Europe. Well, I think that's not good for America. It's not good for our national security. And we – our allies, we have to work together to counter Russia, to counter China, to help us in the Middle East. And it's constant criticism, along with the president's threats towards Greenland, as well as Canada, it's hurt us. Our allies have lost a lot of trust.

So, I don't think these comments by the secretary were helpful.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Well, I know you have been taking a stand against Russia and for Ukraine. You did that this past week, along with some of your colleagues, as you put it in remarks on the House floor, "this is our Churchill moment or our Chamberlain moment and, by God I'm going choose Churchill." Seventeen Republicans joined you. The last time we saw a vote on Ukraine aid, there were 100 Republicans supporting it. What was going on here and how do you get the Senate to take up what you did get over the line?

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: Well, a couple things here.

First of all, the president has had a policy of wanting to negotiate a settlement. I don't think it's working. He has – too much has tried to act like an umpire, trying to work with two different people in a boxing match. But that's not the case. You have a country that's invading Ukraine. They're bombing cities every night. There's a good versus evil here and America should be, you know, unabashedly for the right side here. The democracy, the country that wants free markets, the country that wasn't to align with us.

Russia hates us. I don't know why the president can't see that. Putin hates the United States. He hates what we stands for. So, that's a problem there.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: When it comes to the House, the speaker has not wanted his – not wanted to get in front of the president on this. And so he lobbied pretty hard, and we call whipping, against this vote. And I think he was wrong.

I waited for a year and a half in this Congress to get something done on Ukraine and we've done nothing. There's been no votes, no policies from the leadership here or the president to support a country that's fighting for its life. I agree with the – your previous interview that Ukraine has the upper hand right now, but Russia is bombing those cities every night, and we should be there to help them to defend against these ballistic missile attacks.

The speaker whipped against us, and that's why it drove that number down. I think he was wrong. He says he's pro-Ukraine, but the actions speak louder than words.

MARGARET BRENNAN: President Zelenskyy was on this program last Sunday asking for more interceptors, but also he made clear that he wants friendly countries in Europe who have a good relationship with the U.S. To be able to produce the Patriots, as well. I know your colleague, Mike Turner, wrote to the president last week asking for that part to be delivered on.

Do you support it? I mean, what's the holdup?

REPRESENTATIVE DON BACON: I do support it. We cannot produce enough Patriots right now to handle what we're doing in Iran to provide Ukraine, but also we need to have these same missile defenses in Asia for whether it's North Korea or China, and we're not producing enough. So, we should look for our allies to help create additional production lines. I know Ukraine would love to help do that, and they need these missiles very badly.

What I would do in this case, and we have a low stockpile because of Iran, I would sit down with our allies and just look at what assets we have and come up with a plan to give anti-ballistic missile technology and capabilities to Ukraine. And we can't do it all, but we should sit down with the allies and build a plan to get it done.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Don Bacon, Republican from Nebraska, thank you so much, sir.

We'll be right back.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Should the government regulate A.I. And if so, how?

We're joined by CBS News cyber contributor Chris Krebs, who ran CISA in the first Trump administration, and Ben Buchanan, who advised President Biden and is now a professor at Johns Hopkins and an adviser to Anthropic.

Good to have you both here.

CHRIS KREBS: Good to be here. Thanks for having us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, this was a big change because President Trump and his advisers clearly saw something that led to a shift in their policy. They were very light touch. Literally don't do anything. And now there was this executive order, just a few days ago, to have some step towards, I don't know if we can call it regulating it because it's voluntary, but that the companies have to voluntarily provide their very sensitive technology 30 days before releasing it to let the government have the first look. What does this accomplish, Chris?

CHRIS KREBS: Well, I think the biggest concern was, while there had been a sense that generative A.I. and some of the more advanced tools were giving cyber attackers and defenders better capabilities, it wasn't until about two months ago where Anthropic released their Mythos – or at least announced their Mythos preview that really brought it, I think, to the forefront with cabinet secretaries like Scott Bessent in Treasury and some other folks. They became more concerned. They go to the White House, say, hey, we need to take a bit more of a proactive approach. And so –

MARGARET BRENNAN: They got concerned because business entities –

CHRIS KREBS: Yes, I mean in part the Treasury – the finance sector banks, Jamie Dimon at J.P. Morgan and a number of others were like, whoa, whoa, whoa, we need to pause, we need to think about what we're doing here, and we need to take a bit more robust security-focused approach on how we – as this avalanche of vulnerabilities that will be discovered by A.I., how we prepare and ensure that we're not going to be overwhelmed.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Ben, 30 days for the government to conduct a full security vetting. Is that possible or is this just sort of window dressing to say the government's doing something?

BEN BUCHANAN (Former White House Special Adviser for Artificial Intelligence): In the Biden administration we built a capability at the A.I. Safety Institute to do quick, voluntary testing for A.I. systems, including for cyber risks and for bio risks. So, I think the tests themselves can go quickly. But that doesn't mean the government is going to do that in a fulsome way. So, the jury, I think, is still out on how the president chooses to implement this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

BEN BUCHANAN: But the timing here I think is not one of the pieces that worries me. It's more getting the details of what does this testing look for?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. And what's the consequence?

BEN BUCHANAN: Exactly. Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, like, can the government stop it? The whole risk and worry had been this would get in the way of America's arms race with China. Does this get in the way of America's arms race with China?

BEN BUCHANAN: Not as – not as it's currently written. No, I don't think so. And I don't even think even more stringent versions would.

MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

BEN BUCHANAN: I do think what's happening here is you see the government wrestling with something that we wrestled with in the Biden administration. This technology is coming from the private sector. And in many respects it's the first revolutionary technology that is primarily in its current form from the private sector.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Meaning?

BEN BUCHANAN: Think (ph) about nukes or space or so much more.

MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

BEN BUCHANAN: The government has and has had a role in all of those technologies, inventing them, shaping them. It doesn't really have that in A.I. So, the Trump administration is now trying to figure out, how does it want to assert itself in this new domain that actually is quite different conceptually than many of the ones that came before it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And, in Congress, they haven't regulated really.

CHRIS KREBS: Yes. In fact, the executive order is very clear when it says, this is not a licensing regime. There is not a pre-clearance mechanism. But it does set up a structure where the NSA, the National Security Agency, can define what a covered model is, and then bring those models into a – the 30-day peer (ph) review. And then you can look at maybe what some of the vulnerabilities that could be discovered and then you can share those out with defenders, with industry, so that they are prepared.

But separately this week you had Congressman Obernolte introduce draft legislation that may give a requirement for submitting some of these subsequently covered models for peer (ph) review and auditing by independent bodies on a twice a year basis.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Unclear if that's got a future, though, that legislation.

CHRIS KREBS: But it – but it's starting the conversation, which I think is critical.

MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

So, the president did say to reporters that all the big A.I. leaders are coming to the White House quite soon. He has said he's looking into the U.S. government, taking an ownership stake in some A.I. companies. Meaning, us U.S. taxpayers would own stakes. And it's been reported that OpenAI's Sam Altman also pitched an idea to Senator Bernie Sanders about transferring 50 percent of the equity of the top A.I. companies to a public fund.

To both of you, would that work? What does that do? Is that just retrofitting what you said, which is the government needs to have some kind of hand in here?

BEN BUCHANAN: It's certainly conceptually trying to adjust – address that question of what's the relationship between the public and private sector. I think something that is that drastic, the devil is really in the details and we don't have any details of this meeting or even of Senator Sanders' proposal. So, I think we've got a long way to go in making that real, and it feels, in Congress, with me of, what does it mean to let the private sector run here. So, I think there's a lot of complexity that's yet to be worked out on that proposal.

CHRIS KREBS: And on that note, it also creates a significant governance challenge, you know, when you control, when you own part of – whatever the tool is, it creates a conflict of interest and some self-dealing, perhaps, if you're also trying to regulate it.

So, again, the details here are what's going to matter. It is interesting that it's almost a horseshoe effect where you have both Republicans and Democrats that are talking about, you know, perhaps we need to take an ownership stake in these models.

MARGARET BRENNAN: They seem scared. I mean that seems to be the takeaway that's forcing a change in position. And, I mean, Anthropic, the company you advise, called for an international pause in A.I. development because of how fast the systems are improving. As I understand it, the concerns the models are becoming so advanced they can fix themselves without humans being involved.

BEN BUCHANAN: Well, the dynamic here that's very interesting is what we call recursive self-improvement. So, the A.I. systems help the A.I. companies generate the next version of the system. And that can show up in a number of ways. One of the ways it can show up is the A.I. systems write the computer code for the next version. Another one is the A.I. systems do the research and some of the math and underlying conceptual work that leads to efficiencies in the next system. And now we increasingly see A.I. systems helping design the chips that are the lifeblood of this.

So, I think it is the case for a variety of reasons, recursive self- improvement, massive infrastructure investments. We should expect these systems to get – continue to get very good, very quickly. And that does raise real national security questions no matter who is president.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you expect that most companies are going to comply with this voluntary 30-day review, Chris?

CHRIS KREBS: Well, I think there's a separate mechanism that probably has more teeth. And that's what was issued on Friday, a national security presidential memorandum on the national security enterprise in the use of A.I., which allows the Department of Defense to use the power of the purse. The procurement mechanisms to dictate what the policies are and who needs to submit to reviews and who will, you know, follow certain presidential – or, rather, department-level direction. So, I think the executive order is an interesting framing for a government-wide approach, but the real movement, I think the real teeth is what's happening at the Department of Defense in dictating what the policies are for how vendors can dictate to the government on how models can be used.

BEN BUCHANAN: In the Biden administration in 2023, we brought the companies to the White House to meet with the president and they all made voluntary commitments, which they then followed through on, to do independent red team testing for risks like cyber, for bio, to publish their testing results to the public. And they followed through on that. So, I do think there's a history here of companies working with government, but I suspect both sides are going to have to do a lot more as this technology gets better.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I recall during the Biden administration there was this agreement between the U.S. and China not to let A.I. touch nukes.

BEN BUCHANAN: That's right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: As I understand it –

BEN BUCHANAN: That's right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: There's discussion about the risk towards biological weapons. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google's A.I. initiative signed a letter saying there should be a law to keep A.I. out of bio, biological weapons.

BEN BUCHANAN: Chris spoke very well, and he spoke very well about the cyber dimensions of the current set of models. I would look at these current models not as cyber models but as generally capable models. And the bio frontier is –

MARGARET BRENNAN: What does that mean? Sorry.

BEN BUCHANAN: They can do expert tasks in a wide variety of areas, not just in cyber. Also in bio and the like. This was something that we were very alert to in the Biden administration. There's a long section on bio in the president's executive order in 2023. There's upside. You know, A.I. can do a lot for medical discovery, but there also is legitimate concern that A.I. is outperforming Ph.D. level virologists on virology questions, and that could abet a bio weapon risk. That is not hypothetical.

MARGARET BRENNAN: OK, well now you're scaring me.

I mean do they need to be bilateral agreements between countries or this is because we have the edge at this moment. America needs to set the rules of the world for everyone. I mean essentially they did for nuclear weapons, right? We had – we had them first. But it was out of fear.

CHRIS KREBS: Look, A.I., emerging technologies, quantum is going to present, I think, the same problem. But we're now entering this governance space where technology development is moving faster than democratic oversight and control can allow, or provide.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. They're (INAUDIBLE).

CHRIS KREBS: And I think your earlier question about they're scared, there's fear, it's – it's they're overwhelmed. They don't really understand the technology. It's very complex. Understanding how to meaningfully intervene that's consistent with the American regulatory tradition, that's light touch, free markets, capital markets, we are seeing a bit of a – I think a divide here on how to interact. But again, you are seeing some interesting parallels in direction of travel that's consistent between the administration, the Congress and Democrats and Republicans that understand something needs to be done. We're just not quite sure what the mechanisms are just yet.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. And the technology is moving really quickly while that's being debated.

Gentlemen, thank you for bottom lining this for us.

We'll be right back in a moment.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: On Friday we spoke with Rye Barcott, a Marine veteran who was the founder of With Honor, an organization that supports military and public service veterans for higher office. His new book is "Courage Can Save Us: Ten Extraordinary Americans and the Fight for our Future."

We began by asking about the group's mission and why it's so important now.

(BEGIN VT)

RYE BARCOTT, AUTHOR, "COURAGE CAN SAVE US": We helped recruit and train and help elect veterans to take our pledge to serve with integrity, civility and courage, including the courage to work across party lines at a difficult time to do so.

Through that process, I've gotten to know many of them quite well. And so, what I decided to do was select 10, an even balance of five and five, all of whom were in office at a very difficult, challenging time for the country and really unpack where their courage came from and then look at moments of courage, both in military service, as well as in politics and elected office. Sometimes that courage is quieter, it's more of a moral courage versus a physical courage, which they may have encountered in the military. But that was the – that was my approach to this book, which I've written principally for students. I'd like to see more students being able to study courage. I define courage as a form of service. That is taking risk in the service of something larger than yourself. It's not self- interested. It's serving what's referred to oftentimes as the common good.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you do need to inspire younger people, it sounds like, because when we look at the polling, overall 17 percent of Americans, according to Pew, trust the government in Washington to do what's right all or most of the time. Our own CBS polling has showed the younger generation's dispirited.

BARCOTT: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: They're anxious about their futures. So, how do you inspire them to join a system that they believe is broken?

BARCOTT: Yes. I mean I think a lot of young people are – they're feeling lonely. There's a lack of a sense of purpose. One of the great things that I found through military service was that it gives you a – it gives you some – a sense of something larger than yourself and a common mission with Americans from all different walks of life.

So, one of the key takeaways for the book is to find a – to find a route into public service. And that's one of the goals with this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you worry we are at a point where the kind of moral courage you're describing is nearly impossible to fill? Because when we look at the kind of partisanship out there, and then you look at, for example, the redistricting that may lock in that partisanship and disincentivize the thing you say you want to encourage, bipartisanship, the forces are kind of against you.

BARCOTT: The forces are really going against us. And most Americans want courage but feel like they see very little of it or none of it. And what I wanted to shine a light on is to say that this still exists. It still exists. Here are ten examples of it. It's hard. We need to celebrate it when it – when it arises.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You know, past military service doesn't guarantee a flawless life. I mean you've gestured to that.

BARCOTT: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But we've been talking about this with candidates – the Democratic Senate candidate of Maine, for example, other lawmakers. Do you ever look at candidates and say, despite your service, I can't support you? How do you make that call?

BARCOTT: We do. We only – we usually only do about 10 percent of the overall vets that run. This year there is more vets running than any year before. It's an increase of over 30 percent across party lines. Quite encouraging. Many of those vets are not running in races that are winnable. So, that's one criteria. But really, fundamentally, we look at character. And you have to commit to this pledge to serve with integrity, civility and courage. We watch how people conduct themselves on the campaign trail. We interview individuals that served with them in the military under duress. And it's only about 10 percent of the veterans that make the cut.

Once they serve in office, they really need to be committed to it. They have to – they have to maintain that trust across party lines. That doesn't mean that they'll agree on every issue. Most issues they don't. But they'll maintain trust and relationships. It doesn't always work.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You talk about the pledge. When we looked it up, the pledge is to bring civility to office, participate in a cross-partisan veterans caucus. You asked members also to pledge just to meet with a member of the opposing party once a month and then join them in significant bipartisan legislation.

BARCOTT: That's right. And importantly –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Can we watch (INAUDIBLE) on that?

BARCOTT: I mean it seems to have –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Congress isn't legislating these days.

BARCOTT: Yes. Yes, yes, yes, yes, can we amp it up and expand it more?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

BARCOTT: I hope so. We have continued to grow and maintain that cohesion, but it has been difficult. I mean there have been many moments over the last eight years where we've – where, you know, relationships get frayed. I mean January 6th was one example.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

BARCOTT: You know, many others. And this matters for the country, but it is not easy. And, you know, meeting alone is one thing, but then actually being willing to have the courage to put your name with another and say, we're going to do this and we're going to stand for this, even though I might get attacked for working with the enemy. I mean it's a crazy thing.

There's a – there's a survey out that 80 percent of Republicans and Democrats, registered Republicans and Democrats, of course about 40 percent of the country are non-affiliated. But among those that are a affiliated, over 80 percent refer to the other side as the enemy. I mean that's what we're – and that's why with this book I think courage can save us as a country. The us is the flag. It has a crack in it. It's not broken, but it has a crack in it. We're in a serious place as a nation. We're turning 250 years old. But at the end of the day, I believe this is a – this is an optimistic outlook. There are a lot of people that are still, you know, serving for the good of service. Something that's larger than themselves.

(END VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Our full conversation is on our website, YouTube page and podcast platform.

We'll be right back.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. Thank you all for watching. Until next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.

World.title: Alexander Zverev becomes Grand Slam champion with French Open win
World.content:
Alexander Zverev is no longer one of the best players never to win a major title.

He's finally a Grand Slam champion.

In his fourth major final, Zverev beat Flavio Cobolli 6-1, 4-6, 6-4, 6-7 (5), 6-1 for the French Open title on Sunday.

It was a unique opportunity for Zverev without Jannik Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz across the net and the third-ranked German took full advantage on the red clay of Roland Garros.

When Cobolli missed an overhead on the second championship point after more than four hours of the five-set encounter, Zverev dropped on his back to the clay and covered his face with his hands as he began sobbing. When he got up, with his shirt and arms covered in clay, Zverev put his hands back on his face before he lifted both arms in celebration.

Zverev has now joined an elite group of players that captured their first major in their fourth final: Eight-time major champion Andre Agassi, 2001 Wimbledon winner Goran Ivanisevic and 2020 U.S. Open champion Dominic Thiem.

Alexander Zverev reacts after winning the men's final match at the French Open in Paris, Sunday, June 7, 2026. Aurelien Morissard/AP

No Sinner or Alcaraz

Zverev had been an overwhelming favorite for the title ever since the top-ranked Sinner struggled in the first week's heat wave and wasted a two set and 5-1 lead against Juan Manuel Cerundolo in the second round. A day later, 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic was also eliminated.

Alcaraz, the two-time reigning champion, withdrew before the tournament with an injured right wrist.

It was Zverev's second French Open final, having wasted a lead of two sets to one against Alcaraz in the 2024 championship match.

Zverev had an even bigger advantage — two sets to none — in the 2020 U.S. Open final and lost that one, too, to Thiem. He was also beaten in straight sets by Sinner in the 2025 Australian Open final.

It was the 25th title of Zverev's career.

Cobolli's 1st Slam final

The 14th-ranked Cobolli had never been past a Grand Slam quarterfinal until this week. He was attempting to become the first Italian man to raise the singles trophy at Roland Garros since Adriano Panatta 50 years ago.

Cobolli comes from the same tennis club in Rome as Panatta did and Panatta was asked by tournament organizers to present the Coupe des Mousquetaires to the champion to celebrate the anniversary of his 1976 triumph.

The honors, however, were going to Zverev.

Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva won the women's singles trophy on Saturday.

Alexander Zverev plays in the men's final match at the French Open in Paris, Sunday, June 7, 2026. Christophe Ena/AP

Zverev took control early on

The match was played in perfect conditions and Zverev's game was almost flawless at the start.

Zverev broke Cobolli's serve in a long opening game when Cobolli shanked a forehand into the first row of the stands. The break came after Zverev had a bit of luck when a backhand return hit the net but dribbled over on game point for Cobolli.

A group of women in the stands held up letters to form Zverev's nickname: "Sascha."

Cobolli likes to stand way over near the corner of the court and hit big kick serves out wide into the ad court. Zverev knew what was coming and returned one such kick serve early in the first set with a backhand that he wrapped around the outside of the net post. Cobolli ended up winning the point, but it was a message from Zverev that he knew how to handle his opponent's tactics.

The next time Zverev hit a wrap-around-the-net-post return, Cobolli couldn't handle it and Zverev won the point.

Cobolli's supporters in his box were all dressed in blue, the color of Italy's national teams, and as Cobolli worked his way back into the match, there were chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole; Flavio, Flavio."

After Zverev held for a 6-5 lead in the fourth, he had his upper right leg treated by a trainer. Then Zverev wasted a 3-1 lead in the tiebreaker, which Cobolli concluded with a forehand winner up the line that produced a roar from the crowd.

But Cobolli appeared to run out of energy in the fifth, running down a drop shot only for Zverev to then pass him up the line for a 3-0 lead and a double break.

World.title: Notable Deaths in 2026
World.content:
"Persepolis" author and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi poses during the Rome Film Festival, Nov. 16, 2012. | TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity. By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery. Iranian-French cartoonist and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi (November 22, 1969-June 4, 2026) won worldwide acclaim for her graphic bildungsroman "Persepolis," which told the story of a young girl coming of age in Tehran in the midst of her country's Islamic Revolution. First published in French beginning in 2000, the multiple-volume memoir became an international bestseller, and later an Oscar-nominated animated film – one denounced by the Iranian government. Illustrated in black-and-white, "Persepolis" was the tale of a rebellious young girl growing up in a complicated, aristocratic family that opposed the Shah, but then became disillusioned with the revolution. Relatives faced execution from both sides. "I wanted to show, as an insider, how I lived it," Satrapi told "Sunday Morning" in 2008, "without wanting to make a lesson of history or of politics, or whatever. Not at all. Just to say, in my life, from my point of view, that is the way I lived the thing." Born in Rasht, Iran, and raised in Tehran, Satrapi was sent by her parents to Europe as a teenager for her education, away from the restrictions imposed upon women in her homeland. She was an art student in Strasbourg when she devised "Persepolis," despite little experience in comics. It sold millions. Satrapi was then offered the chance to turn her graphic novel into an animated film. She assembled a team to draw all the animation by hand. For her animators, she acted out all the parts, from a dog to an old man, her grandmother, and herself. She got Catherine Deneuve and her daughter, Chiara Mastroianni, to provide voices. The resulting film was nominated for an Academy Award. Living in Paris with a Swedish husband, Satrapi directed several more features (including "Chicken With Plums," "The Voices" and "Radioactive"), while also writing graphic books ("Embroideries," "Woman, Life, Freedom") and children's stories ("The Sigh," "Monsters Are Afraid of the Moon"). Despite living in exile, Satrapi remained an optimist, telling "Sunday Morning," "We don't have the right to become cynical. I want to keep the stars in my eyes, and still believe that it's possible. Human being is capable of the worst. But human being is also capable of the best."

Peabo Bryson Peabo Bryson performs at Radio City Music Hall in New York City, Sept. 13, 1991. | Ebet Roberts/Redferns via Getty Images Singer Peabo Bryson (April 13, 1951-June 2, 2026) was famed for his R&B hits, including many collaborations with Roberta Flack (such as the 1983 song "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love"). He also sang the duets "Beauty and the Beast" with Céline Dion, and, from "Aladdin," "A Whole New World" with Regina Belle, both of which won Oscars for best song (and earned Bryson two Grammy Awards). Born and raised in South Carolina, Bryson started performing with traveling revues, and appeared on Moses Dillard and Tex-Town Display's 1969 album "Now!" He then built a solo career that included "Reaching For The Sky," "Feel the Fire," "I'm So Into You," "Let the Feeling Flow," "If You're Ever In My Arms Again," and the #1 R&B hits "Show & Tell" and "Can You Stop the Rain." He also recorded with Natalie Cole ("Gimme Some Time"), Minnie Riperton ("Here We Go"), Melissa Manchester ("Lovers After All"), and Kenny G. ("By The Time This Night Is Over"). Bryson also appeared on stage in productions of "Raisin," "The Wiz" and "Porgy and Bess." In 2007 Bryson told CBS' "Saturday Early Show" that his song "Missing You" (the title track of his 20th soul album) was an emotional tour de force for him: "When you strip away everything and are left with just a piano and what God has given you, you tell a deeper story," he said. "The words for this beautiful song made me think of the two women I love the most in this world, my mother and my sister, both of whom I lost. When I sing the line 'I can't wait to see you again this side of Heaven,' it's for them. This song is for anyone that you've ever loved in a real way."

Marcia Lucas Marcia Lucas, seen with her then-husband director George Lucas, holds the Academy Award she won for editing "Star Wars," at a post-Oscar party in Los Angeles, April 4, 1978. | AP Photo Academy Award-winning film editor Marcia Lucas (Oct. 4, 1945-May 27, 2026) was married to George Lucas and worked on several of his films (along with those of Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese). She was widely credited with having "saved" "Star Wars" when it came to putting together the film's dogfight sequences in the climactic Battle of Yavin – an amalgamation of miniatures, explosions, World War II-style cockpit dialogue, a heroic mercenary, and a bit of the Force. Marcia was an apprentice editor working with the legendary Verna Fields when she met George, then a USC film student, in the late 1960s. They married, and Marcia worked as an assistant editor on George's debut feature, "THX-1138." Marcia then shared an Oscar nomination, with Fields, for editing "American Graffiti." Her views on the space fantasy "Star Wars" were particularly important to George, who leaned on her counsel when – halfway through production – she convinced him to kill off Obi-Wan Kenobi on the Death Star, a fact George hid from the studio. She also suggested Princess Leia give Luke Skywalker a kiss "for luck" before swinging over a deep chasm. She eventually took over editing duties when George expressed unhappiness with an English editor who'd started a rough cut of the film. George told Rolling Stone in 1977 that the film's final battle scene over the Death Star – fashioned after World War II movie dogfights – was extremely hard to edit: "Marcia can normally cut a whole reel – all ten minutes of the film – in one week. I think it took her eight weeks to cut that battle. It was extremely complex and we had 40,000 feet of dialogue footage of pilots saying this and that. And she had to cull through all that, and put in all the fighting as well. Nobody really has ever tried to interweave an actual plot story into a dogfight, and we were trying to do that, however successful or unsuccessful we were." Marcia shared the Academy Award for "Star Wars" with Paul Hirsch and Richard Chew, and followed with editing "The Empire Strikes Back" and "Return of the Jedi." (The Lucases divorced after "Jedi" was released.) Her counsel was also vital for other directors' work. When an early version of Steven Spielberg's "Raiders of the Lost Ark" (which George has co-written and produced) was screened, after all the congratulations, Marcia spoke up: What about Karen Allen's character, who was last seen tied to a stake with Indiana Jones when the Nazis were vanquished? A concluding scene where Indy and Marion go for a drink had been written, and yet, "They never shot it, because they didn't think they needed it," Marcia recalled in a 2017 interview. "I said, 'I don't want to leave Marion on the stake! You need to do that!" So, George flew the actors to San Francisco and shot the last-minute addition at City Hall. Marcia's other credits included Coppola's "The Rain People"; Haskell Wexler's "Medium Cool"; Scorsese's "Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore," "Taxi Driver," and "New York, New York"; and Michael Ritchie's "The Candidate."

Sonny Rollins A portrait of jazz musician Sonny Rollins dating form the 1950s. | Bob Parent/Getty Images Like his contemporaries, John Coltrane and Charlie Parker, tenor saxophonist Sonny Rollins (Sept. 7, 1930-May 25, 2026) was revered for his improvisational acuity, and his eagerness to pursue innovation in an art form that he helped define. His experimental works, captured in such recordings as 1956's "Saxophone Colossus" and his 1962 live album "Our Man in Jazz," influenced generations. He also collaborated with the greats, from Miles Davis, Dizzy Gillespie and Freddie Hubbard, to the Rolling Stones (appearing on their 1981 album "Tattoo You"). One of the leaders of the bebop era, Rollins told the Associated Press in 2007 that he found it "excruciating" to listen to what he deemed flaws in his older recordings. "I don't consider myself a musician that has learned as much as I want to learn," he said. Born into a musical family in Harlem, he hadn't even finished high school when he was invited to join Thelonious Monk's band. Soon he was recording with Miles Davis and Bud Powell. But a heroin addiction led to jail sentences, a drug treatment program – and a spiritual awakening. "I began to have a deeper philosophy of what life was about," he told the AP. "From that point on is when my consciousness awoke." After being discharged, he joined the Max Roach-Clifford Brown quintet, before recording his "Saxophone Colossus," heralding the arrival of a leading sound in hard bop. Other notable albums included "Way Out West," "A Night at the Village Vanguard" and "Freedom Suite." He also recorded music for the Michael Caine film "Alfie." Rollins referred to himself as "a work in progress," adopting new styles of performance, and frequently taking time out to hone his skills away from the stage. In 1959, he retreated from performing, spending months practicing on a walkway on the Williamsburg Bridge (to avoid annoying his Lower East Side neighbors). "It was a great experience," he told "The Early Show" in 2011. "Almost a religious experience." That long sabbatical led to his 1962 album "The Bridge." He continued to tour into his 80s, until health issues forced his retirement from playing. His 61st album, "Road Shows, Vol. 4: Holding the Stage," was released in 2016. A Kennedy Center Honoree in 2011, he won two Grammys, for best jazz instrumental album (2000's "This Is What I Do") and best jazz performance ("Why Was I Born?," recorded in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, which occurred just a few blocks from his apartment). "The thing that I am most proud of in my career is that fact that I was able to see beyond being popular and all that stuff," he told the AP in 2007, "and do what my inner self told me to do."

Ted Turner Ted Turner announces the launch of CNN in Atlanta, June 1, 1980. | Rick Diamond/Getty Images He was, in the words of his third wife, actress Jane Fonda, "a gloriously handsome, deeply romantic, swashbuckling pirate." Ted Turner (Nov. 19, 1938-May 6, 2026) was a businessman, sportsman and conservationist. Eager to take risks, and with an outsized personality and penchant for being outspoken, Turner reshaped the media landscape, and highlighted the importance of environmental protection. His early notoriety came via sports. A four-time winner of the Rolex Yachtsman of the Year award, Turner reportedly won more than 500 major sailing trophies. He was skipper of the racing yacht Courageous, whose crew won the America's Cup in a four-race sweep in 1977, earning him the nickname "Captain Courageous." In the 1970s, he bought the Atlanta Hawks and the Atlanta Braves. After the Braves suffered a 17-game losing streak, Turner put on a uniform and took over as manager. Commissioner Bowie Kuhn banned him from the field the next day. The son of the owner of several radio stations and a billboard advertising firm, Turner inherited the company after his father's death and turned a failing business profitable. He then acquired an undistinguished UHF TV station, WTCG, whose signal was too weak to even cover most of Atlanta. With an old movie library, reruns like "The Andy Griffith Show," cartoons, and broadcasts of baseball, basketball and hockey games, Turner built it into a "superstation" by making its signal available free to cable systems across the United States. Renamed WTBS, the channel joined basic cable lineups viewed by approximately five million cable subscribers. (That figure would grow to more than 90 million.) Turner's greatest television achievement was founding the Cable News Network, the first all-news-all-the-time TV channel. Born from Turner's frustration at not being able to find news on TV late at night, CNN helped establish the 24-hour cable news cycle — a revolutionary moment that transformed the industry. By the time of the 1991 Gulf War, CNN was broadcasting live from Iraq and Saudi Arabia during the early hours of the war, with the network showing images of the attack on Baghdad. In the 1980s, Turner acquired MGM/UA. Using the studio's library of more than 4,000 films, he launched Turner Classic Movies and TNT, while the Hanna-Barbera animation library led to creation of the Cartoon Network. He also purchased the film production companies New Line Cinema and Castle Rock Entertainment. (He failed in a bid to take over CBS.) His fortunes rose and fell. In 1996 he sold Turner Broadcasting System to Time Warner for $7.3 billion in stock. When AOL and Time Warner merged in 2001, Turner's stock value rose in the billions. After the merger, stock prices plummeted. "[I lost] seven or eight billion," he told "60 Minutes" in 2003. He quit his job as vice chairman, which he described as "a title without portfolio ... like the emperor of Japan." Asked what it felt like to look at CNN from the outside, Turner said, "It's difficult. But you know, you can't live in the past. You've got to live in the present and the future. And I've got plenty to do." Much of that was focused on philanthropy, conservation and habitat restoration. He owned two million acres — an amount of land larger than the state of Delaware — and turned them into living laboratories to help preserve the nation's largest bison herd, as well as elk, whooping cranes, Rio Grande Cutthroat trout, black-footed ferrets, the Bolson tortoise, and other imperiled species. To support what he termed "eco-capitalism," he opened up his ranches to tourism, and in 2002 started a restaurant chain, Ted's Montana Grill, that served bison burgers. He founded the Nuclear Threat Initiative, which advocated for non-proliferation; donated $1 billion to found the United Nations Foundation, an independent charitable organization supporting causes such as children's and women's health and human rights; and founded and sponsored the Goodwill Games, an Olympic-styled event meant to counter the boycotts of the Cold War. In addition to co-creating and co-writing "Captain Planet and the Planeteers," an animated children's series promoting care of the environment, in 1989 he funded the Turner Tomorrow Fellowship Award, which bestowed a half-million-dollar prize for an unpublished novel that promoted "creative solutions to humanity's urgent problems." "See, my life is more an adventure than a quest to make money," Turner once said. "Adventure is going out and doing something for the pure hell of it. You just want to see if you can do it, period. There's no thought of gain other than your own satisfaction."

Michael Tilson Thomas Michael Tilson Thomas conducting the USC Symphony at Bovard Hall, at his alma mater USC, Oct. 5, 2009. | Lawrence K. Ho/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images For conductor and composer Michael Tilson Thomas (Dec. 21, 1944-April 22, 2026), known for his swashbuckling charm at the podium, performing was in his blood. His paternal grandparents, Boris and Bessie Thomashefsky, were considered the "Burton and Taylor" of Yiddish theater. But while he was surrounded by art and music from birth, and received lessons at an early age from the likes of Igor Stravinksy and Jascha Heifitz, the prodigy said his parents did not want him to go into the performing arts; they encouraged him to become a scientist instead. But in high school, he found his true calling when his music teacher failed to make class one day. Thomas put down his oboe and picked up the conductor's baton. He discovered he preferred being the orchestral leader. "I didn't like practicing very much," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2025. "And I could get very good results as a conductor very quickly." At 25 he made his New York debut when he took over for an ailing conductor at a Boston Symphony concert. The "boy wonder" received early praise from his mentor Leonard Bernstein, and two years later became music director of the Buffalo Philharmonic in 1971. That same year he began conducting the New York Philharmonic's "Young People's Concerts." He also co-founded the New World Symphony, a teaching orchestra, in Miami, and was music director of the San Francisco Symphony for 30 years. In a 1984 "Sunday Morning" profile, Thomas described himself as "an adventurous romantic. I'm interested in all kinds of things. I'm interested in experimentation. I'm interested in exploration. I'm also interested very much in tradition, and this is just the way I am." Which explained Thomas' passion not just for the masters of the classical repertoire, such as Mahler, Beethoven and Gershwin, but also for contemporary composers like Steve Reich and John Adams — and rock legends James Brown, Elvis Costello and Metallica. His discography includes nearly 150 albums. Thomas also composed music; his works include pieces featuring texts by Walt Whitman, Emily Dickinson, and Anne Frank. In an extended interview with "Sunday Morning," Thomas described his function as a conductor: 'I'm kind of like the captain of a ship. So, we're on this ship together and we're on the high seas and we're traveling along and all at once we come to an island. This is a completely uncharted island, not on any map. And it's just crawling with all kinds of animals, creatures that are not described in any encyclopedia or anything anywhere. They're all completely unknown and they're making all these sounds which are completely unrecognizable. Wouldn't that be the most thrilling thing that could possibly happen? Wouldn't that be a lot more interesting than saying, 'Well, we stopped at this great island which had the most unknown duty-free shopping spot on Earth.' Wouldn't that be better? That's what I'm trying to present, to give you the opportunity to experience music in that way in this kind of discovery mode."

Ruth Slenczynska Pianist and former child prodigy Ruth Slenczynska, at age 33 (left) as she embarked on a nationwide tour in 1958; and right, at age 97. | Bettmann Archive/Getty Images; Meredith Truax/Decca Records Hailed as one of the greatest child prodigies since Mozart, Ruth Slenczynska (Jan. 15, 1925-April 22, 2026) played her first concert when she was 4. She was performing internationally at an age when most kids were learning their times tables, and was mentored by some of the 20th century's greatest virtuosos, including Sergei Rachmaninoff. After she filled in for the Russian composer at a concert when she was just 9 years old, he gave her a Fabergé egg necklace. But her musicality came at a cost. Born in Sacramento to a Polish immigrant father who'd had limited success as a violinist, she was forced by her dad to practice for nine hours a day beginning at age 3. "I wanted to be one of those kids who played," she told "Sunday Morning" in 2022. "And if I didn't practice, I was chased around the apartment with a stick, my father's magic stick. I didn't want that." She quit performing at 15 and later ran away from home. After eloping and then divorcing, she made a living teaching, and in her late 20s returned to the concert stage. She said she wanted to resume her career "as a musician, not a curiosity." Recordings followed, as did television appearances, playing duets with President Truman, and a memoir, "Forbidden Childhood," about her life as a child prodigy. Slenczynska was praised for her impeccable technique. Critics wrote of her "intellectual insight and emotional spontaneity," and her ability to convey the classical repertoire with "rhapsodic freedom." She taught at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, where she served as artist-in-residence for 23 years. It was where she met her second husband, James Kerr, a political science professor. Even after retiring from the university, she continued to give master classes and private lessons; perform internationally; and record for radio and commercial releases. Her 19th album, "My Life in Music," was issued in 2022, when she was 97. Asked by "Sunday Morning" where she is mentally when she performs a recital, Slenczynska replied, "I go to a place I can't take anybody because it's a place from where I get my music."

Alan Osmond American singer Alan Osmond c. 1974. He was the eldest of the popular family singing group The Osmonds. | Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images; Doug McKenzie/Getty Alan Osmond (June 22, 1949-April 20, 2026) was the eldest sibling of what became the popular family singing group The Osmonds. He was also a songwriter, penning such hits as "Down By the Lazy River" and "Crazy Horses." Alan and three brothers — Wayne, Merrill and Jay — were originally a boys barbershop quartet performing at state fairs in Utah. They made their first TV appearance in 1962 on "Disney After Dark," and became regulars on "The Andy Williams Show." The Osmonds went on to release 25 studio and live albums. Younger brothers Donny and Jimmy also joined the group, and later became solo artists. In the early 1970s the group hit its peak, with six gold albums and seven Top 20 hits, including "One Bad Apple," "Yo-Yo," "Down By the Lazy River," "Hold Her Tight," "Crazy Horses" and "Love Me For a Reason." As the group's songs veered from bubblegum pop to rock, Donny Osmond became a breakout star, and also teamed with sister Marie for recordings and a TV variety show, which Alan produced. In the 1980s, Alan, Wayne, Merrill and Jay regrouped as a country act, releasing "One Way Rider." Their hits included "I Think About Your Lovin.'" At the time, Alan told The Associated Press he switched from recording rock to country music because it better fit their wholesome image. "Country music really is the backbone of America," he said. "It doesn't just come and go. And we're kind of flag-wavers. You find that in the country area, too." He also helped lead Stadium of Fire, an annual July Fourth celebration in Provo, Utah, that is one of the largest in the country. Four of Alan's own children formed another group, The Osmond Boys, also known as The Osmonds Second Generation. In 1987, Alan was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and in the late '90s retreated from touring. He helped create the Children's Miracle Network, which aids children's hospitals, and with his wife Suzanne founded the humanitarian organization OneHeart. Doug Osmond, one of Alan's sons, told The AP of his dad: "I've never met anyone more positive in my life. I never once heard him complain, not once. He would say, 'I may have MS, but MS does not have me.' That was his motto and he always was worried about everyone else. ... Family always took priority and his faith was in everything he did."

Desmond Morris Desmond Morris with the chimpanzee Congo on the TV program "Zoo Time," 1956. | Desmond Morris Collection/Universal Images Group via Getty Images As a young boy, English zoologist Desmond Morris (Jan. 24, 1928-April 19, 2026) watched his father slowly die of wounds suffered during World War I. Affected by humanity's inhumanity, he became fascinated with the animal world — studying zoology and animal behavior — and art. He became a curator of mammals at the London Zoo, and a television presenter. A surrealist painter himself, Morris even gave a paintbrush to a chimpanzee named Congo. The resulting work is said to have delighted Picasso. One chimp painting sold at auction for £14,400. In 1967 Morris wrote "The Naked Ape," a look at the evolution of man and how human behavior compared to that of other primates — including sexual selection and mating habits. "I spent the first half of my life studying animal behavior," Morris told The Guardian in 2007, "and when I eventually wrote a book about human beings, I wrote about them as if I was writing about another animal species. … I hadn't any hopes for it; I didn't expect it to do anything. People say I must have known what I was doing. They think I deliberately wrote it to make a shocking bestseller, but it wasn't like that." The book was a sensation, selling more than 20 million copies, but was also criticized as being patriarchal. Nearly four dozen books followed, including "The Human Zoo," "Intimate Behavior," "Manwatching" (about body language), "The Soccer Tribe," "Catwatching and Cat Lore," "Dogwatching," and "Babywatching." There were also books on surrealist art. "I should have stuck at the art," Morris told The Guardian. "I think I had the potential to be a good artist. I still consider myself a serious artist but a very minor one, and I'm a minor artist because I've been doing too many other things. My strength is that I do lots of different things; my weakness is that I don't stick at any of them long enough."

Bob Hall Bob Hall competes in the 1978 Boston Marathon. | Frank O'Brien/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Bob Hall (Oct. 31, 1951-April 12, 2026), who lost the use of his legs from polio during childhood, became known as the father of wheelchair racing, recognized as the Boston Marathon's Wheelchair Champion three times. Hall was not the first to compete in the Boston Marathon in a wheelchair; in 1970, Eugene Roberts, who'd lost both legs in the Vietnam War, completed the course, unsanctioned, in more than six hours. But in 1975, organizers promised Hall a finisher's certificate if he could complete the 26.2-mile distance in less than three hours. His finishing time: 2:58.00. "It had nothing to do with, per se, the marathon, but it was about the inclusion," Hall told The Associated Press last year, on the 50th anniversary of his pioneering ride. "It was that I was bringing people along." Hall won again in 1977 (at 2:40:18), besting seven fellow male and female wheelchair competitors, when Boston was designated the site for the National Wheelchair Championship. Hall received encouragement along the route from marathon winner Bill Rodgers and fifth-place finisher Tom Fleming, who both slowed to encourage him. "The interaction was a sign that we were fully accepted as athletes," he said. He sued in 1978 to have wheelchair racers admitted into the New York Marathon, where it would be more than two decades before men's and women's wheelchair divisions were created. Hundreds more wheelchair athletes have followed Hall, many using racing chairs he built. In Boston this year, 50 wheelchair racers competed, along with 50 others in para and adaptive divisions. "Because of him crossing that finish line, we're able to race today. And it's evolved so much since then," five-time Boston winner and eight-time Paralympic gold medalist Tatyana McFadden told The AP last year. "It was him. It was him being brave and saying, 'I'm going to go out and do this because I believe that we should be able to race Boston Marathon just like everyone else.' So he had the courage to do that."

Pearl Fryar Pearl Fryar in his topiary garden in Bishopville, S.C. in 2017. | Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images "The moment you work a cut above average, you will be recognized for that," self-taught topiary artist Pearl Fryar (Dec. 4, 1939-April 4, 2026) told "Sunday Morning" in 2005. "And I was a person that wanted some recognition in my lifetime." The recognition he initially sought, after he and his wife Metra moved into a ranch house in Lee County, S.C., was to win the local garden club's Yard of the Month Award, owing to his carefully landscaped and decorated front lawn and flower beds. It turned out Fryar wasn't even eligible; his house was outside Bishopville's city limits. But he didn't give up. "Now I got to come up with some way to make them make an exception, and that's how I got into topiary," he said. Fryar, who'd never heard the word "topiary," got a three-minute lesson from the owner of a local nursery on how to prune a plant. With a gas-powered hedge trimmer in his hands, Fryar was transformed — and so was his property. "Just started cutting everything I had in my garden," he said. "Pine trees, oak tree, it didn't make any difference, I started cutting." Out of a former cornfield he created a three-acre topiary garden, filled with plants and shaped into whimsical living sculptures — trees carved into fish, mushrooms and sailing ships. Hedgerows bubble up; plants twist and spiral towards one another. He carved the words "Love, Peace, and Goodwill" into the lawn. In January 1985, Fryar came home from work one day and found the sign reading, "Yard of the Month." "I went out screaming, because I had accomplished my goal," he said. "They left it for three months and they came out and they said to me, 'Well, we can't give it to you anymore because you're professional.'" Fryar's topiary garden, now overseen by a nonprofit organization, contains 400 topiaries, alongside junk art sculptures. It would take two weeks for the heralded "Picasso of Plants" to trim his whole garden — engaging in what he called "yard aerobics" — before starting all over again, all while also working at a beverage can manufacturing company. After his retirement (he said work interfered with his hobby), Fryar gave tours of the grounds, which attracted 10,000 visitors a year. And it had a spillover effect; Fryar's neighbors began shaping their landscapes, too, because, how could you not? The pleasure Fryar gave, and got back, made all the trouble worthwhile. "In my garden, you see a lot of love and hearts and 'I love you,' and I think one of the greatest things in the world is to say to someone `I love you,' you know? And in a sly way, that's what I have done."

Mary Beth Hurt Mary Beth Hurt as Helen in 1982's "The World According to Garp." | Warner Brothers Actress Mary Beth Hurt (Sept. 26, 1946-March 28, 2026) appeared in about two dozen New York productions, earning three Tony Award nominations for "Trelawny of the Wells," "Crimes of the Heart" and "Benefactors." An Iowa native (her babysitter was future actress Jean Seberg), Mary Beth Supinger studied at New York University's graduate theater program and performed in regional theaters, where she met her first husband, William Hurt. Upon graduation, she performed in West London with The Questors theater troupe, and in New York at Joseph Papp's Public Theater, starring in "As You Like It." She made her Broadway debut in 1974 in "Love for Love" — co-starring another actress making her Broadway debut, Glenn Close. She made her feature film debut in Woody Allen's drama "Interiors" (playing the sister of Diane Keaton and Kristin Griffth) and appeared in "The World According to Garp" (opposite Robin Williams), "Slaves of New York," "The Age of Innocence," "Six Degrees of Separation," "Autumn in New York" and other features. After divorcing William Hurt, she married film director Paul Schrader, and appeared in his films "Affliction" and "Light Sleeper." "I've never been extremely comfortable playing the lead in a play," Hurt told Theater Life in 2010. "I don't like the responsibility; there's a feeling that I have to be good. Besides, I found secondary parts much more interesting, especially when I was younger and the ingénue roles were pretty bland. I never felt very beautiful, or incredibly smart or witty, so I was always looking for something about them that intrigued me. And I would sort of twist that character in a way, because I remember thinking that an ingénue character doesn't ever think they're an ingénue. They think they're a person and they have idiosyncrasies. Those idiosyncrasies interested me." One lead role she did have on film: providing the voice of Jean Seberg, her childhood babysitter, in the 1995 biopic "From The Journals of Jean Seberg."

Dash Crofts Dash Crofts, of Seals & Crofts, performs at Georgia Tech's Alexander Memorial Coliseum, October 22, 1977 in Atlanta. | Tom Hill/WireImage via Getty Singer-songwriter Darrell "Dash" Crofts (Aug. 14, 1938-March 25, 2026) and Jim Seals were native West Texans and high school friends who had played together in various groups before teaming up as a duo, Seals & Crofts. Beginning in the late '60s, when they first opened for such acts as Chicago, Eric Clapton, and the Guess Who, Seals & Crofts' soft rock songs — blends of pop, country, jazz and folk — included such Top 10 hits as "Summer Breeze," "Diamond Girl" and "Get Closer." Other hits included "I'll Play for You," "Hummingbird," "We May Never Pass This Way (Again)," "Goodbye Old Buddies," and "You're the Love." Both had embraced the Baha'i faith, which advocated for global unity, and the religion's themes were woven into their music. "Some people have called it religious music," Crofts told Stereo Review in 1971. "It's not actually religious music, though it is inspired by religion. But no particular musical group influenced us, and I think that's one of the reasons that what is coming out is really us. … We've been in the hard rock scene for a long, long time, and we never mind hearing it and being around it. But playing it gets to be pretty tough physically after a while. … It's such a nice relief to just sit and play pretty stuff for a change." They created controversy with their 1974 anti-abortion ballad "Unborn Child," released the year after the Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. Wade. Although the album was certified gold, numerous radio stations refused to play the song, and protesters picketed. By the early 1980s, with soft-rock going out of fashion, Seals & Crofts were dropped by their label, and they broke up. In 1991 Crofts told the Los Angeles Times that he walked away from recording: "I was completely out of good material. What I had was so bad that we said: 'Why spend the money to go in and (record) this, knowing that nobody's going to like it, and we're not pleased with it?' If it isn't something you respond to yourself, you can't get that excited about doing it for others." But the two later reunited to tour, and in 2004 recorded the album "Traces." Crofts also recorded the 1998 solo album "Today." Jim Seals died in 2022. Crofts told the Times, "Lyrically, I think music can convey things that are hard sometimes for people to say to each other. But through a song, through someone else's eyes, they can see it and it's not so much a confrontation." Music also permeated their families. In the 1970s, Jim's brother, Dan Seals, teamed up with Croft's high school classmate, John Ford Coley, to record together as England Dan & John Ford Coley ("I'd Really Love to See You Tonight"). In 2010, Seal's daughter, Juliet Crossley, and Crofts' daughter, Amelia Dailey, formed a group called the Humming Birds. And in 2018, Seals' cousin Brady and Crofts' daughter Lua formed the duo Seals & Crofts 2.

Chip Taylor Chip Taylor performs at the 47th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony, at the Marriott Marquis Hotel in New York, June 9, 2016. | Charles Sykes/Invision/AP Born James Wesley Voight (his brothers are Academy Award-winning actor Jon Voight, and world-famous geologist Barry Voight), musician and songwriter Chip Taylor (March 21, 1940-March 23, 2026) was best known for the songs made famous by others: "Wild Thing," recorded by The Troggs and Jimi Hendrix; "Angel of the Morning" by Merilee Rush and Juice Newton; "Try (Just a Little Bit Harder)" by Janis Joplin; and "I Can't Let Go" by The Hollies and Linda Ronstadt. "When I started writing hits, it was a very proud period of time that I had," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2001. "I mean, I loved the fact that other people would record my songs." But he wanted to record his own songs as well. Beginning in 1971, he released several solo albums, including "Chip Taylor's Last Chance," called one of the best country albums of the year by Rolling Stone. But seven years later, a dispute with his record label — when they refused to promote what he thought would be a hit single — led him to leave music and take up gambling, which had been a part-time hobby. For nearly 15 years, he called New York's Belmont Park home. Gambling became his muse, and his livelihood. "It was a fun job," he said. In the mid-1990s, he restarted his music career when his mother was dying of cancer. "My mom got very ill, and that was the real turning point," he said. "I decided one day instead of going to the racetrack to go down and play some songs for mom to make her feel a little better. So, I guess I missed [it] a little bit. Spending the real good quality time with my mom that one day gave me the spirit to do it the next day — not for Mom but for us, for Mom and me. … And I'd go up to my little recording studio, which had been left dormant for pretty much all the time, and I started recording a couple of things." After his mother's death, Taylor stuck with his music, releasing 25 albums beginning in 1996. He launched his own recording label, Train Wreck Records, and toured the U.S. and Europe. And while Taylor's songwriting gifts continued to be appreciated (in 2001 the reggae artist Shaggy released a new cover of "Angel of the Morning," which hit #1 on the Billboard Chart), his brother Jon Voight wondered at what cost: "Well, you had to know that he has a genius for gambling. You have to understand, there's a lot of talent there that is really being laid to waste now. I mean, there's nothing but songs, songs, songs. I mean, how many hours a day do you have to keep working on songs?"

Valerie Perrine A portrait of Valerie Perrine as Eve Teschmacher in the 1978 film "Superman." | Hulton Archive/Getty Images Fate and luck (good and bad) marked the trajectory of Academy Award-nominated actress Valerie Perrine (Sept. 3, 1943-March 23, 2026). In 1969, one month before her wedding, her fiancée, a gun collector, accidentally shot himself, fatally. Later that year, while working at the Stardust Hotel in Las Vegas as a topless dancer, she was invited to a party in L.A.'s Benedict Canyon, but bowed out when she could not get an understudy to perform for her. That party would be the site of the Manson Family murders, where Sharon Tate and Perrine's then-boyfriend, Jay Sebring, were murdered. Several years later, Perrine survived a small plane crash in the Pyrenees while traveling to the San Sebastian Film Festival. The tragedies and near-misses of her early years were bookended with a Parkinson's diagnosis that ended her acting areer — one that had seen her win BAFTA, Cannes Film Festival and New York Critics Circle awards for her performance in Bob Fosse's "Lenny," playing the wife of comedian Lenny Bruce. She earned a best actress Oscar nomination for the role as well. Born in Galveston, Texas, her Army dad brought Valerie and her mother, a showgirl, to Japan. There, at age 4, Valerie began performing with a ceremonial dance troupe. But after relocating to Arizona, the family finances suffered, and Valerie left for Las Vegas at 17. "I wanted to show off," she told the Hollywood Reporter in 2023. Afte working as a showgirl, she transitioned to acting, making her film debut in 1971's "Slaughterhouse-Five," based on the Kurt Vonnegut novel, and appearing in several TV movies before landing "Lenny." She was best known as Eve Teschmacher, the assistant to arch villain Lex Luthor, in the first two "Superman" films opposite Christopher Reeve. Perrine, who was afraid of water, said that she'd drunk "a whole bottle of champagne" before filming a scene in which she dives into a pool to rescue, then kiss, the drowning Man of Steel. "I'm a desert girl," she explained. Other credits included "W.C. Fields and Me," "The Magician of Lublin," "The Electric Horseman," "Can't Stop the Music," "The Border," "Maid to Order," "Bright Angel," "Sweet Bird of Youth," and "What Women Want," as well as TV appearances including "Northern Exposure," "Burke's Law," "Homicide: Life on the Street," "ER," "Nash Bridges," "The Practice," "Walker, Texas Ranger," "As the World Turns" and other series. The 2019 documentary "Valerie," directed by her longtime friend Stacey Souther, traces her life and the Parkinson's that robbed her of much mobility. "No matter what life gives you, you have to fight," she said. But she did not sound regretful: "I think I've done it all."

Robert Mueller Former Special Counsel Robert Mueller testifies before Congress about the Russia-Trump investigation, on July 24, 2019. | Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Robert Mueller (Aug. 7, 1944-March 20, 2026), a former Marine, served as a United States attorney, deputy attorney general, and director of the FBI. He investigated white collar crimes, bank fraud, and state-sponsored terrorism, and led prosecutions of mob boss John Gotti, Panamanian leader Manuel Noriega, and the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. But his most high-profile role was as a special counsel, tasked to investigate Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and its possible connections with the campaign of President Trump. His probe, which was completed in 2019, operated under restrictions imposed by a White House legal counsel opinion that a sitting president could not face criminal charges. Mueller, however, reiterated that a president could be charged once he'd left office. His team did not depose Mr. Trump, however, fearful that court fights over a subpoena would have delayed the investigation further. Mr. Trump claimed that the report, released in a redacted form in the spring of 2019, cleared him of wrongdoing. However, Mueller wrote in an introduction about whether Mr. Trump had obstructed justice: "If we had confidence after a thorough investigation of the facts that the President clearly did not commit obstruction of justice we would so state. … [W]hile this report does not conclude that the President committed a crime, it also does not exonerate him." Federal charges were levied against 34 people, including 25 Russian nationals, and three Russian companies. In his report, Mueller wrote that while the evidence did not establish that Mr. Trump was involved in an underlying crime, "the evidence does point to a range of other possible personal motives animating the President's conduct. These include concerns that continued investigation would call into question the legitimacy of his election and potential uncertainty about whether certain events—such as advance notice of WikiLeaks's release of hacked information or the June 9, 2016 meeting between senior campaign officials and Russians—could be seen as criminal activity by the President, his campaign, or his family." He added, "The President launched public attacks on the investigation and individuals involved in it who could possess evidence adverse to the President, while in private, the President engaged in a series of targeted efforts to control the investigation." In July 2019, Mueller was called to testify before congressional panels. He merely reiterated the report's findings – that the investigation did find that "the Russian government interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion," through disinformation and document leaks whose goal was "supporting the Trump campaign and disparaging candidate Hillary Clinton." Mueller did confirm that Trump campaign officials (including Carter Page, George Papadopoulos, Michael Flynn, Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner and Paul Manafort) all had contacts with Russians. However, he did not establish that they "conspired or coordinated" with the Russian government. Regarding a June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower in New York City, during which Donald Trump Jr., Paul Manafort and Jared Kushner discussed the release of potentially damaging information about Clinton with a Russian lawyer, Mueller said he could not prove the participants knew their conduct was illegal at the time the meeting took place. He said shifting explanations about why the meeting took place had been made to "avoid political consequences." Republicans called the FBI's investigation into Trump's ties with Russia, which had predated Mueller's probe, politically motivated, accusations Mueller denied, calling the investigation and the people who conducted it "fair and independent." He chose to let the report speak for itself, and rarely gave interviews. But in 2024, he provided the introduction to a book, "Interference: The Inside Story of Trump, Russia, and the Mueller Investigation," written by lawyers who'd served on his team. "The evidence was clear that the Russian government engaged in multiple, systematic attacks designed to undermine our democracy and favor one candidate over the other," Mueller wrote. "We were not prepared then and, despite many efforts of dedicated people across the government, we are not prepared now. This threat deserves the attention of every American. Russia attacked us before and will do so again."

Chuck Norris Chuck Norris in the TV series "Walker, Texas Ranger," in 1997. | CBS via Getty Images Martial arts grandmaster and action hero Chuck Norris (March 10, 1940-March 19, 2026) started his training in judo and Tang Soo Do while deployed with the Air Force as an MP in Korea. He became a six-time undefeated world professional middleweight karate champion and launched a movie and TV career that spanned more than 30 action films and the long-running CBS series "Walker, Texas Ranger." After receiving his honorable discharge in 1962, Norris worked at Northrop Aircraft as a clerk and opened a martial arts studio in Redondo Beach, Calif. He developed his own Korean-based American hard style of karate, known sometimes as Chun Kuk Do. The studio became a chain. One student, Steve McQueen, encouraged him to get into acting. After an uncredited role as a bodyguard in the Dean Martin film "The Wrecking Crew," he received his first credited role in the Hong Kong martial arts film "The Way of the Dragon," opposite Bruce Lee, followed by "Yellow-Face Tiger," playing a San Francisco drug lord. He was then top-billed in a string of popular movies, including "Breaker! Breaker!," "Good Guys Wear Black," "A Force of One," "The Octagon," "An Eye for an Eye," "Forced Vengeance," "Lone Wolf McQuade," "Missing in Action," "Code of Silence," and "The Delta Force." Meanwhile, in the late 1970s he'd founded the United Fighting Arts Federation. In 1985 he told CBS News' "West 57th," "Think of this: Here I was, a kid who never excelled in any sports in school. I was too small. So, I get into karate and I become a world karate champion. Here's a kid who could not even get in front of a class and give a book report, all the way through school, and now I'm an actor." For nine seasons, beginning in 1993, he starred in the CBS series "Walker, Texas Ranger," which he described to the Associated Press as "fighting injustice with justice, good vs. bad." He followed the advice of McQueen, who'd told him, "Don't talk unless there's something to say." "I don't like dialogue that much anyway," Norris told CBS. "It's not in me to be a Dustin Hoffman or a Laurence Olivier. I enjoy the action, because I'm physical. And I enjoy the basic heroic image that I project, that I think is a good image for kids to see. "The difference between violence and action is the philosophy when you use it," he said. "What I mean there is, if I provoke something, and I get into a physical thing because I've provoked it, I consider that violent. But if I'm put into a position where I have no way of getting out of it except through action or fighting, then there's a certain philosophy there, because the kids say, 'Well, he didn't look for it.'" While his "tough guy" image made him an icon, it also sparked internet parodies. The viral "Chuck Norris Facts" posed absurd statements alluding to Norris' tough-guy image, such as "When the Boogeyman goes to sleep every night, he checks his closet for Chuck Norris;" and "Chuck Norris can slam a revolving door." He ultimately embraced the ridiculousness of the memes and penned "The Official Chuck Norris Fact Book," which raised money for a nonprofit (co-founded with President George H.W. Bush) to promote martial arts instruction for children. "To some who know little of my martial arts or film careers but perhaps grew up with 'Walker, Texas Ranger,' it seems that I have become a somewhat mythical superhero icon," he wrote. "I am flattered and humbled." In 2012 Norris joined fellow action movie stars Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Jet Li and Jean-Claude Van Damme in "The Expendables 2." With a wink to his internet memes, Norris' character, a retired military operative named Booker, confirmed that he'd once been bitten by a king cobra: "But after five days of agonizing pain, the cobra died."

Alexander Butterfield White House aide Alexander Butterfield at the swearing-in before the Senate Watergate Committee in July 1973. | Steve Northup/Getty Images In July 1973, White House aide Alexander Butterfield (April 6, 1926-March 9, 2026) gave dramatic testimony to a Senate committee investigating Watergate. When asked if he was aware of any listening devices in the Oval Office, Butterfield replied, "I was aware of listening devices, yes, sir." Butterfield, who served as deputy assistant to President Nixon, actually oversaw the secret, voice-activated taping system that was installed in the White House, in Nixon's office in the Executive Office Building, and at the presidential retreat at Camp David. According to Butterfield, it was known only to himself, Nixon, chief of staff H.R. Haldeman (an old college friend of Butterfield's) and several Secret Service agents. Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward had tried and failed to interview Butterfield, and so he passed his name on to the Congressional committee, who brought him in to testify.
